trees__binary-tree-maximum-path-sum.title: Binary Tree Maximum Path Sum
trees__binary-tree-maximum-path-sum.pattern: Post-order DFS returning single-branch gain, updating a global max
trees__binary-tree-maximum-path-sum.statement: A path is any sequence of connected nodes where each node appears at most once; it need not pass through the root. Return the maximum sum of values over any non-empty path.

approaches.name: DFS returning single-branch gain
approaches.idea: For each node compute the max downward gain of a path starting at that node and extending into at most one child (`node.val + max(0, leftGain, rightGain)`, clamping negative child gains to 0). Separately, the best path *bending* at this node joins both children: `node.val + max(0,left) + max(0,right)`; use that to update the global answer. Return only the single-branch value so the parent can extend it.

trees__binary-tree-maximum-path-sum.insight: Two quantities: what you RETURN (one branch, to extend the parent) vs what you RECORD (both branches joined here). Clamp child gains at 0 to drop negative subtrees.

trees__serialize-and-deserialize-binary-.title: Serialize and Deserialize Binary Tree
trees__serialize-and-deserialize-binary-.statement: Design an algorithm to serialize a binary tree to a string and deserialize that string back to the identical tree structure.

examples.explanation: serialize then deserialize reproduces the tree.

approaches.name: Preorder with '#' null markers
approaches.idea: Serialize by a preorder walk, emitting each node value and a sentinel `#` for every null child, comma-separated. This fully encodes structure so no second traversal (like inorder) is needed. Deserialize by consuming tokens in the same preorder order from a queue: `#` yields null, otherwise build a node then recursively read its left and right subtrees.

trees__serialize-and-deserialize-binary-.insight: Preorder + explicit null sentinels uniquely determines a binary tree, so one traversal round-trips it; consume tokens in the same order to rebuild.

trees__construct-binary-tree-from-preord.title: Construct Binary Tree from Preorder & Inorder
trees__construct-binary-tree-from-preord.pattern: Recursion using preorder root + inorder split, with index map
trees__construct-binary-tree-from-preord.statement: Given `preorder` and `inorder` traversals of a binary tree with unique values, reconstruct and return the tree.

examples.explanation: 3 is root; 9 is left, 15/20/7 form the right subtree.

constraints: preorder and inorder consist of unique values
inorder is a permutation of preorder

approaches.name: Preorder pointer + inorder index map
approaches.idea: The first unused preorder value is always the current subtree's root. Its position in inorder splits inorder into the left subtree (before it) and right subtree (after it). Advance a single global preorder pointer and recurse on the left inorder range first (preorder visits left before right). A hash map from value to inorder index makes each split O(1), giving overall O(n).

trees__construct-binary-tree-from-preord.insight: Preorder gives the next root in order; inorder position of that root partitions left vs right. Recurse left before right to keep the preorder pointer aligned.

trees__lowest-common-ancestor.title: Lowest Common Ancestor
trees__lowest-common-ancestor.pattern: Post-order recursion returning where p and q are found
trees__lowest-common-ancestor.statement: Given a binary tree and two nodes `p` and `q`, return their lowest common ancestor: the deepest node that has both `p` and `q` as descendants (a node can be a descendant of itself).

examples.explanation: 5 and 1 are on opposite sides of the root 3.

constraints: p != q and both exist in the tree

approaches.name: Single post-order DFS
approaches.idea: Recurse: return the node itself if it is null, `p`, or `q`. Otherwise take the results from both subtrees. If both sides return non-null, this node is where the two targets meet, so it is the LCA. If only one side is non-null, propagate that result upward. This finds the answer in one pass without parent pointers.

trees__lowest-common-ancestor.insight: The LCA is the first node where p and q are found in different subtrees; a node matching p or q short-circuits upward.

trees__binary-tree-cameras.title: Binary Tree Cameras
trees__binary-tree-cameras.pattern: Greedy post-order with 3 states (needs cover / covered / has camera)
trees__binary-tree-cameras.statement: Each camera on a node monitors its parent, itself, and its immediate children. Return the minimum number of cameras needed to monitor every node of the tree.

examples.explanation: One camera on the middle node covers all nodes.

approaches.name: Greedy bottom-up placement
approaches.idea: Return one of three states per node: 0 = uncovered, 1 = covered but no camera here, 2 = has a camera. Place cameras as late as possible (near leaves' parents): if any child is uncovered, this node must hold a camera (state 2); else if any child has a camera, this node is covered (state 1); otherwise it is uncovered (state 0) and defers to its parent. A null child returns 1 so leaves are treated as uncovered. Finally, if the root is left uncovered, add one camera.

trees__binary-tree-cameras.insight: Push cameras onto parents of leaves, not leaves themselves; a null returns 'covered' so leaves stay uncovered and force a camera one level up.

trees__vertical-order-traversal.title: Vertical Order Traversal
trees__vertical-order-traversal.pattern: DFS with (row,col) coords, ordered by col then row then value
trees__vertical-order-traversal.statement: Return the vertical order traversal of a binary tree: group nodes by column (left to right); within a column order by row (top to bottom); nodes sharing the same row and column are ordered by increasing value.

approaches.name: Coordinate DFS + sorted maps
approaches.idea: Assign each node a coordinate: root is (row 0, col 0); a left child is (row+1, col-1) and a right child is (row+1, col+1). Collect values into a `TreeMap` keyed by column, whose values are `TreeMap`s keyed by row, whose values are a min-heap (or sorted list) of node values. Iterating the nested sorted structures yields columns left-to-right, rows top-to-bottom, and ties broken by value.

trees__vertical-order-traversal.insight: Sort by (col, row, value) exactly in that priority; nesting TreeMap>TreeMap>min-heap bakes the ordering in so no explicit comparator sort is needed.

trees__recover-binary-search-tree.title: Recover Binary Search Tree
trees__recover-binary-search-tree.pattern: Inorder traversal to find the two swapped nodes
trees__recover-binary-search-tree.statement: Exactly two nodes of a BST were swapped by mistake. Recover the tree by restoring it to a valid BST without changing its structure.

examples.explanation: Nodes 1 and 3 were swapped; swap their values back.

approaches.name: Inorder scan for inversions
approaches.idea: An inorder traversal of a valid BST is strictly increasing. Two swapped nodes create either one adjacent inversion (`first` = the larger, `second` = the smaller, adjacent) or two inversions (`first` = the larger of the first drop, `second` = the smaller of the second drop). Track the previous node during inorder: on the first inversion set `first = prev` and `second = cur`; on any later inversion update `second = cur`. Swapping the two nodes' values fixes the tree.

approaches.name: Morris inorder (O(1) space)
approaches.idea: Same inversion logic, but use Morris traversal to walk inorder without recursion or a stack: temporarily thread each node's inorder predecessor's right pointer to it, then unthread on the second visit. This achieves O(1) extra space, which is the follow-up ask.

trees__recover-binary-search-tree.insight: Inorder must be sorted; the two swapped nodes are the endpoints of the inversion(s): first = the higher value seen first, second = the lower value seen last.

trees__count-of-smaller-numbers-after-se.title: Count of Smaller Numbers After Self
trees__count-of-smaller-numbers-after-se.pattern: Fenwick tree (BIT) over ranks, scanning right to left
trees__count-of-smaller-numbers-after-se.statement: Given an integer array `nums`, return an array `counts` where `counts[i]` is the number of elements to the right of `nums[i]` that are smaller than `nums[i]`.

approaches.name: Binary Indexed Tree over compressed ranks
approaches.idea: Compress values to ranks via a sorted copy. Scan `nums` right to left, maintaining a Fenwick tree of already-seen ranks. For each element, query the prefix count of ranks strictly less than its own rank — those are the smaller elements already inserted (i.e. to its right) — then insert its own rank. This is grouped under Trees because a Fenwick/segment tree is the classic structure here; a merge-sort counting inversions is an equivalent O(n log n) alternative.

trees__count-of-smaller-numbers-after-se.insight: Scan right to left and count how many smaller ranks are already inserted; a Fenwick tree makes each prefix-count and insert O(log n).

trees__all-nodes-distance-k-in-binary-tr.title: All Nodes Distance K in Binary Tree
trees__all-nodes-distance-k-in-binary-tr.pattern: Build parent links, then BFS outward from target
trees__all-nodes-distance-k-in-binary-tr.statement: Given a binary tree, a `target` node, and integer `k`, return the values of all nodes that are exactly distance `k` from the target node, in any order.

examples.explanation: Nodes 7,4 (down) and 1 (up via root) are distance 2 from 5.

constraints: target is a node in the tree

approaches.name: Parent map + BFS
approaches.idea: A binary tree only has downward pointers, so first record each node's parent with a DFS. Then treat the tree as an undirected graph and BFS outward from `target`, expanding to left child, right child, and parent at each step while tracking visited nodes. After `k` levels the queue holds exactly the nodes at distance `k`.

trees__all-nodes-distance-k-in-binary-tr.insight: Add parent pointers to make the tree an undirected graph, then it is a plain BFS-by-levels stopping at level k.

trees__maximum-sum-bst-in-binary-tree.title: Maximum Sum BST in Binary Tree
trees__maximum-sum-bst-in-binary-tree.statement: Given a binary tree, return the maximum sum of node values of any subtree that is itself a valid Binary Search Tree. The empty subtree is allowed, so the answer is at least 0.

examples.explanation: The subtree rooted at 3 with children 2 and 5 (and 4,6) is a BST summing to 20.

approaches.name: Bottom-up BST validation
approaches.idea: With one post-order pass, return four facts per subtree: whether it is a BST, its min value, its max value, and its sum. A node forms a BST only if both children are BSTs and its value is strictly greater than the left subtree's max and strictly less than the right subtree's min. When valid, update the global best with the combined sum and return the merged (min,max,sum); otherwise mark not-a-BST so ancestors are disqualified. Empty children return isBST with +INF min / -INF max so any node compares correctly against them.

trees__maximum-sum-bst-in-binary-tree.insight: Carry (isBST,min,max,sum) up in one post-order pass; a node is a BST iff both subtrees are and val lies strictly between left.max and right.min.
